item.title: [ABC News World] Ukrainian President Zelenskyy presses Western allies for postwar security guarantees
item.description:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy presses Western allies for postwar security guarantees
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his government is seeking specific security guarantees from Western allies for post-war supportByDEREK GATOPOULOS Associated PressNovember 6, 2026, 5:58 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his government is looking for specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function when the nearly-five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of his nation finally ends.
Zelenskyy's comments in an interview aired late Thursday came after two days of discussions among allies concluded in Brussels that focused on post-war security and reconstruction, and days before planned three-way talks next week in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States, the first trilateral peace discussions since February.
While talks on the contours of peace continue, the grim reality of war remained front and center Friday in Ukraine, with more Russian drone attacks and a rising death toll from Moscow's guided bomb strike Monday on a former school operating as a humanitarian aid distribution center.
Two days of talks in Brussels discussed postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government’s Western allies. The meetings brought together officials from the U.S., U.K., France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the U.S. investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post.
“We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote.
In his television interview, Zelenskyy said he wants to see tangible results.
“What matters is that it’s clear on paper,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine’s private 1+1 television broadcast late...

item.title: [ABC News World] South Africa's ruling ANC faces huge decline in support, early election results show
item.description:
South Africa's ruling ANC faces huge decline in support, early election results show
South Africa's African National Congress faces a significant decline in voter support, according to interim results from local elections held this weekByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 6, 2026, 5:47 AM
JOHANNESBURG -- South Africa's long-dominant African National Congress party was set to lose significant voter support and control of some major cities in local government elections held this week, interim results across the country showed on Friday.
South Africans voted this week in local polls that determine which parties get to control major cities and local municipal districts that are responsible for the delivery of basic services like water, road maintenance and rubbish removal.
With 76% of votes counted nationally, the ANC had garnered nearly 31% and was lagging behind rival parties in key cities like Johannesburg, Tshwane and eThekwini.
During the last local government elections in 2021, the ANC received just over 45% of votes nationally. Its worst electoral performance was in 2024 national elections, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time.
ANC spokesperson Mahlengi Bhengu on Friday acknowledged the latest results show the party was losing significant voter support.
“We are conscious of the message that our voters, especially our historical voters, are conveying to us. And we are going to have a serious, honest and deep reflection about how to rebuild the confidence between ourselves and the people of South Africa,” Bhengu said.
The ANC has dominated electoral support in South Africa since the country's first democratic elections in 1994 but has experienced a steady decline.
It formed a unity government with the rival Democratic Alliance and smaller political parties, while at the local level it governs some cities through coalition governments.

item.title: [BBC World] Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern FranceByJames GregoryPublished6 November 2026, 09:32 GMTUpdated 20 minutes ago
One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.
The driver is reported to have been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Earlier, French education minister Édouard Geffray said the crash involved students.
He told reporters it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
French Transport minister Philippe Tabarot, who was on his way to the area, said more than 100 firefighters had also been sent.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

item.title: [BBC World] Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
item.description:
Image source, EPAByMax MatzaPublished6 November 2026, 01:20 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument.
"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
The order does not prevent future presidents from changing the decor of the famous room.
The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.
The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.
The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.
How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image
Signing the new executive order on Thursday, the president said: "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country."
He added that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.
Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone.

item.title: [CBS News World] French workers flood streets for anti-government protests
item.description:
Tens of thousands of government workers, teachers, transport employees and other union workers in France walked off the job Thursday to take part in the latest round of massive economic protests that have roiled the European nation, expressing their frustration with low wages and the high cost of living.
What was billed as a national day of action started with nearly 200 peaceful rallies across the country.
The General Confederation of Labour, or GCL, one of France's major unions, said that about 1.6 million people took to the streets, while France's Interior Ministry pegged the number much lower, at about 600,000.
Demonstrators march through Paris on Nov. 5, 2026, as part of a general strike.
Clement Souchet/NurPhoto via Getty Images
The demonstrations even briefly shut down the Eiffel Tower.
"Our salaries do not allow us to live anymore," Sophie Binet, the head of GCL, told CBS News when asked why the ongoing demonstrations have taken center stage in France.
Binet urged supporters to continue the protests and accused French President Emmanuel Macron of not hearing the people's cries for help.
"Because he thinks he knows everything alone," Binet said of Macron. "Because he works for the rich, for the … multinational and for the finance, not for the working people."
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday called for a meeting with the unions, but another protest is already scheduled for this coming Saturday.

item.title: [Guardian China] UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
item.description:
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, pictured in 2019, is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city. Photograph: Jérôme Favre/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, pictured in 2019, is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city. Photograph: Jérôme Favre/EPA
UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.
Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.
The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

Pro-democracy umbrella movement protesters on the streets of Hong Kong in 2014. Photograph: Alex Hofford/EPA

item.title: [BBC China] Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Joshua Wong jailed for 10 yearsByAbel U, BBC Chinese, Reporting fromHong Kong and Kelly NgPublished5 November 2026
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory
Published30 November 2024
What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong
Published18 December 2023
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was in his early teens.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September.

item.title: [Guardian China] Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece
item.description:
Unforgettable … Gong Li in Raise the Red Lantern. Photograph: Era International/Kobal/Shutterstock
View image in fullscreen
Unforgettable … Gong Li in Raise the Red Lantern. Photograph: Era International/Kobal/ShutterstockReview
Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece
Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama
Revisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong, is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism.
Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film.

item.description:
Joshua Wong in 2019. He gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP
View image in fullscreen
Joshua Wong in 2019. He gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
View image in fullscreen
A prison van believed to be carrying Joshua Wong arriving at the high court in Hong Kong on Thursday. Photograph: Vernon Yuen/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

item.title: [Guardian World] British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
item.description:
The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP
View image in fullscreen
The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP
British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.
A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

item.title: [Guardian World] ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
item.description:
A voter casts their ballot in Lawley township, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. Photograph: Oupa Nkosi/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
A voter casts their ballot in Lawley township, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. Photograph: Oupa Nkosi/Reuters
ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).
“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”
Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.
Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.

item.title: [BBC China] Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
item.description:
Image source, PNG East New Britain Province Facebook pageImage caption,
The 32kg object was found at a construction site in Port MoresbyByKelly NgPublished4 November 2026
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

item.title: [BBC China] Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
item.description:
Image source, VCG/VCG via Getty ImagesByOsmond Chia, Business reporter and Angus ThompsonPublished30 October 2026
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

item.title: [Guardian World] Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
item.description:
Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffectiveBy Rachel Savage in Durban Deep
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.
“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
View image in fullscreen
Cora Bailey, who founded the charity Claw, has encountered illegal miners since 1991. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian
Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.
